This game is currently in the Humble Bundle for April 2021. If you are interested in the game and it's before May 4th, 2021, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.

After an playing an hour of Simulacra and Simulacra 2 to review for the Humble Choice April 2021 Bundle:

These are a pair of horror or thriller games.  The first game spooked me with a major opening that has a lot of horror elements in it, but then didn’t do much with the horror aspect in the next 40 minutes.  Instead, it focused more on what life would be like as a woman.

Simulacra has you find a woman’s phone and then try to figure out what happened to her.  Though while playing it I noticed how freaking awful it would be to be a woman.  There’s a solid social commentary on how some people spoke to the mystery girl online and it’s done in a very strong way.  This isn’t social commentary being forced in there, but instead a strong point the game makes. 

The gameplay is mostly about snooping on the phone and has voyeuristic qualities to it.  You can even impersonate her with different people, and it’s quite interesting.  As much as I dislike the horror aspect in the beginning because I’m a scaredy-cat, I found myself wanting to play more as it’s more of a thriller.

Simulacra 2 seems to up the production values but presents a very similar experience.  Though I do want to mention there are a few grammar issues that I noticed in both games, and apparently, the team who created the game is from Malaysia, which might explain that.  Nothing that bad, but it can be a bit noticeable. 

Pick this up if you like horror or thriller, these aren’t long games, but they are unique.  There are some effective and interesting moments, such as hearing a woman’s voice from behind you if you’re playing wearing headphones. 

If you enjoyed this review or want to know what I think of other games in the bundle, check out the full review on or subscribe to my youtube channel:

https://youtu.be/KQoCrsCpfF0

A supernatural horror story where you use a missing person's phone (texting contacts/viewing photos/reading e-mail/other apps or social media) to figure out what happened to them. Not the same but it gives a similar feel to me as a game like Orwell.

I don't really enjoy horror games in general so I preferred playing this game as a mystery. I didn't really care for the random 'horror' sound effects or imagery. I was a bit disappointed when the plot went for [spoiler]the sci-fi twist. It's alright but I would have liked a regular, more realistic thing. It felt like something outside of your control with no real foreshadowing or buildup. There is nothing to suggest that it was possible and even after you learn about it you can't go back and see much in a new light. It might be nice if they at least put something random about the dangers of AI or something.[/spoiler]

Aside from the general phone-searching there are some minigames. They aren't too tough but one might be harder if you're not a native english speaker. One minigame is taking a jumbled list of words and making the right sentence out of it. However, it's not enough to get an equivalent meaning- you have to get the word order exactly right. For example, 'Meet me and I'll show ya this weekend' is wrong but 'Meet me this weekend and I'll show ya' is right.

Worth a look if you're fine with learning about the missing person story through phone history and dialogue.

Other thoughts:[list]
[*] It's a little annoying that in order to get the 'good' ending you have to [spoiler]manipulate people because there's no way to convince them otherwise.[/spoiler]
[*] I would have liked multiple save slots.
[*] It's nice that it can be set to automatically skip text on repeat playthroughs.
[*] Pretty much no settings to adjust (only subtitles). I would've liked at least volume and resolution options.
[*] Some inconsistencies/strange things: [spoiler]She met Taylor on Spark but had been following him on Jabbr 3 months ago. Cassie's AMA from 3 months ago is still continuing even though it closed (you get to ask a question)? The article mentions a back-and-forth between genders but you're forced to repeat the female gender and use one of the three pre-selected photos (it seems like other pictures don't progress the story). Why is it assimilating the 'weak'? From what I understand it's somehow taking control of a person and building a world out of their simulacrum (online personification?)? And then discarding the physical body for some reason because they can only lure in one person on Spark before they're useless?[/spoiler]
[*] A bunch of grammar and spelling errors and incorrect subtitles.
[*] Only crashed randomly once.
[/list]

review_text_raw:
I'm going to divide this review into various sections based on gameplay elements, in a slightly illogical order. This seems appropriate for a slightly illogical game. Also, I ran out of characters, so I had to leave a lot out.

[h2] Sound Design [/h2]
Best part of the game. Only thing that makes it scary.

Even for someone who had quite a few scares spoiled for me due to watching previous playthrough snippits and common internet knowledge, the scares still all GOT ME. And, I mean, they GOT ME. I was jumping in my seat and looking around for the voices I was hearing. At one point [spoiler] I heard a door knocking and thought someone was trying to break into my bedroom [/spoiler]. Those sounds that play, whether phone ringing or human breathing or that terrible [spoiler] wood knocking [/spoiler], were still enough to make me jump after four straight playthroughs. Every time, I'd finish, and I'd think, this is no Doki Doki Literature Club, I can get through this without jumping. But then there'd be a cellphone ringing or glitched sound or Anna breathing at me and, however slight, I'd jump. The sound in this game was so effective it almost wasn't fair. 

That said, the only thing that was what I can only accurately describe as mid was the voice for the [spoiler] Simulacra [/spoiler]. I'll go into this later, but I got to the end of the game so freaked out by the sound at the beginning, that this didn't leave much an impact.

[h2] Music [/h2]
There isn't as much to gush about here. I'd say it does its job and the title screen is iconic.Part of me wishes I had some more songs to add to my gamer Main Character Syndrome Spotify playlist, but I also do think limiting the soundtrack and sticking to eiry silence cut off by that terrifying sound design is the way to go.

[h2] Characters [/h2]
If I ever found a missing person's phone, and everyone treated me like this, I'd either 1. Say she's better off missing or 2. Just hand the phone off to the cops. 

[h3] Anna [/h3]
They really try to make her sympathetic. She's rejected from vet school and she's just gotten out of a toxic relationship, her workplace is awful and she's being harrassed by her boss and coworker. Now, with all that laid out, you might be wondering, what don't you like about her? She's clearly very layered and passionate and look at all the bad stuff happening to her. She's so sympathetic!

Yes, there are lots of bad things happening to her. But other than the fact that she likes animals and is really bad at picking people to be around, I can't tell you one thing about her. She's just very bland. Honestly, I wonder if it would be more interesting if it was Greg we were supposed to find. Be told by everyone how important it is to hunt him down and bring him back, slowly uncovering that he's not that great of a person, having to contemplate with the consequences of what it would mean to actually bring the jerk back. Anna being the one we need to bring back is just kind of...eh? These people really want her back in their lives and whole time I was just wondering, why? She's cardboard. 

[h3] Taylor [/h3]
He tells bad jokes but you can tell deep down he's got a big heart. He's made some big mistakes and honestly comes off as a bit of a creep. I wasn't sure what exactly he liked about Anna, but that's beside the point. Actually, yeah, that is my only gripe with him. Why is he so invested in the life of a chick he's talked to on a dating app one time? I mean this man goes to her and begs for her and puts himself in danger for her. That's a lot of work for cardboard you saw on sale on Ebay. 

[h3] Greg [/h3]
People like to rip on the actor for this guy, and yeah, I get it. I'm not sure if I was supposed to be laughing at him or if he was supposed to tick me off or if heaven forbid he was supposed to scare me, but he did two of three (i'm sure you can guess which ones). I think Greg sees Anna as someone who he can easily control and manipulate. Which makes sense. She is cardboard. I did find it odd on one route where he [spoiler] suddenly abandons pursuing Anna as soon as he learns the cops are after him [/spoiler]. It came out of left field and then you never learn what happens to him from that point. Honestly, I love to hate Greg, so I think he does his job. I can understand him being obsessive over Anna since 1. they dated for two years and 2. she sees her as easy. 

[h3] Ashley [/h3]
THIS GIRL TICKED ME OFF. I'm not talking about the route where you [spoiler] lie to her and manipulate her into saying she's in love with Anna, though again I ask WHY [/spoiler]. I'm talking about how she treats you if you come clean right away and just tell her who you are and why you have Anna's phone. She flips, gets super defensive. won't let you explain yourself, and then calls the cops on you. She'll randomly disappear from the plot and go offline, and she won't work with you no matter what you say to her. I find that highly improbable. I don't think they knew what to do with Ashley for the routes where [spoiler] she knows the truth [/spoiler].

[h3] Everyone else [/h3]
Nothing much to report. No one made me as mad as Anna's supposed BFF. So good job.

[h3] Simulacra [/h3]
Alright, I have an issue. This thing isn't scary. There's so much buildup, then it's just kind of there. It's so melodramatic and easy to make fun of. I almost think this story would've been better of Greg had just killed her or something. I don't understand how this thing kills or kidnaps, I'm not scared of it, and it keeps changing the rules. I dunno, I just wanted one last big scare, or something that felt satisfying after all that buildup. Then I saw it, and I thought, that's it?

[h2] Story [/h2]
In this game you find a phone that is clearly possessed, and are tasked to find its owner, Anna. You are helped and hindered by the various people trying to get ahold of her, and you can either leave her life in shambles for her to return to or make her life better with your interference. 

Some aspects were rewarding. I liked getting to put that one workplace creep in his place. I liked when I got her a new job in that one playthrough.

I think the main issues with the story were already discussed in the characters section. I don't think the payoff was satisfying. I think I see what they are going for, with the good ending that is. You have to become a master manipulator to take down the manipulator, I do like that. Again, I just felt like the final boss was an absolute joke. I thought it was fake, there was another boss behind the boss, or something. I think the plot excels in relationship drama and just making terrible people act terrible. It's guilty pleasure level entertaining. It gets lost in the big ideas and trying to be bigger than it actually is. I think if it had stuck to a nitty gritty found phone horror game, with people as its worst enemy, it would've stuck the landing a bit more.

[h2] Theme [/h2]
Dating apps bad. Something about valuing the real world over the virtual. Game certainly doesn't punish you much for becoming a master online troll catfishing manipulator. But maybe...maybe that's the real point. We can look back at a preinternet time and recognize that certain things were better back then. But the fact of the matter is, that world doesn't exist anymore. 

Wow. That went deeper than I thought. Too bad the villian sucks and I don't care about Anna. 

[h1] Wait, didn't you recommend this game? I'm confused [/h1]
Yes. I do.

I think it's fun. Fun like watching the Scream franchise. Fun like a haunted hayride sponsored by a high school, where you know things are corny, but you know what, for those couple of times they made you jump, it was worth spending a couple bucks for a ride. Just wait for a Steam sale and get it for like a dollar like I did. This was a really well spent dollar.

review_text_raw:
[h1]Short but Intuitive Mystery Game[/h1]

[i]SIMULACRA[/i] is a modern FMV game that features great sleuthing gameplay with some minor horror elements. After I 100% the entire game, I can safely say this is one of the better indie visual novel titles I've encountered if not for the gameplay alone. I will try to keep this review mostly spoiler-free, but as usual with my reviews for narrative-based games, I will have spoilers for stuff I feel the need to comment on. 

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[olist]
[*] The gameplay and puzzles are fun yet intuitive. I like the process of fixing corrupted messages and images to not only progress the game but to also discover more about the characters.
[*] Lots of "show don't tell" moments that exemplify how the developers understand that this is a visual medium and that it is important to use the visuals to their advantage. For example, though it's never stated Anna is into fitness, one of the first image puzzles is of her posing with weights to give the idea that she is an active person. This is great  yet subtle storytelling I love to see in these types of games. 
[*] The text messages and dating profiles are pretty genuine. There are definitely people out there who act exactly like the ones in this game.
[*] The narrative does a lot to try and make you question the motives of the characters and their backgrounds in a meaningful way so that the suspense is maintained the entire playthrough. 
[*] [spoiler] The main antagonist being a serial killer HAL-9000-esque AI in the phone itself is fascinating in its own right, and the fact that its goal is to create perfect versions of otherwise "pathetic worms" as it refers to people it deems as as such, is great social commentary on how people are obsessed with their public image online to the point that they are no longer genuinely themselves. The antagonist also serves as a personification of tech companies and their obsession to mold people into their idealized image through deceptive practices and establishing trust by packaging things in digestible ways. For example, during the phone reset, the soothing sounds and use of cool hues is meant to contrast with the otherwise invasive questions and disturbing content the OS system tries to get you to answer in detail. In the end, you get the best ending by impressing the AI with your ability to manipulate the characters--an interesting moral dilemma to say the least!  [/spoiler]
[*] The menus and apps look and feel like their real version counterparts. Very good overall graphical presentation. 
[*] Small and subtle changes to show you are progressing through the story. For example, [spoiler] Anna's picture in the home screen will change expression the closer you get to the ending of the game. [/spoiler]
[*] Lots of small things to discover just by exploring the phone (which you can get achievements for). 
[*] Sped up dialog loading for additional playthroughs is a great QoL feature. 
[/olist]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[olist]
[*] The voice acting and FMV sequences come across as cheesy most of the time, if not overacted. 
[*] The autosave feature means you can't go back to a previous part like you can with most visual novels. This means that if you messed up on a certain decision, you may have to restart the entire run just to redo it. This can be pretty frustrating. 
[*] No option to skip puzzles for additional playthroughs means you'll have to do them over and over again which can be pretty tedious if you're trying to get all the achievements. 
[*] The dialogue choices you  need to appease and have Taylor trust you come across as a bit too flirty at times.
[*] Greg and Ashley come across as too angry and distrustful to the player character depending on certain choices made. Meanwhile, Taylor comes across as too trusting. This is why sometimes it's not very good to have a faceless protagonist--we don't really understand what the characters see in [i]you[/i] when the interactions are so minimal. 
[*] The horror elements are too on the nose with the jumpscares. Though the phone OS does have some good subtle horror elements, more of this throughout the game would have been way better overall. 
[*] [spoiler] Though I like the idea of the antagonist, having it type in predictable shaky font and using distorted visuals is pretty cliche. Personally, I think it'd come across scarier if it were way more subtle like how it is when the phone resets.[/spoiler]
[/olist]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Worth at least one playthrough--though playing it blind is your best bet. The gameplay alone makes it worth it. For additional playthroughs, some patience is required. Watch additional endings via recordings if that's not your thing.

[/spoiler] [*] Lots of small things to discover just by exploring the phone (which you can get achievements for). [*] Sped up dialog loading for additional playthroughs is a great QoL feature. [/olist] [h1]Cons[/h1] [olist] [*] The voice acting and FMV sequences come across as cheesy most of the time, if not overacted. [*] The autosave feature means you can't go back to a previous part like you can with most visual novels. This means that if you messed up on a certain decision, you may have to restart the entire run just to redo it. This can be pretty frustrating. [*] No option to skip puzzles for additional playthroughs means you'll have to do them over and over again which can be pretty tedious if you're trying to get all the achievements. [*] The dialogue choices you need to appease and have Taylor trust you come across as a bit too flirty at times. [*] Greg and Ashley come across as too angry and distrustful to the player character depending on certain choices made. Meanwhile, Taylor comes across as too trusting. This is why sometimes it's not very good to have a faceless protagonist--we don't really understand what the characters see in [i]you[/i] when the interactions are so minimal. Personally, I think it'd come across scarier if it were way more subtle like how it is when the phone resets.[/spoiler] [/olist] [h1]Conclusion[/h1] Worth at least one playthrough--though playing it blind is your best bet. When you are a mature person and your childhood and carefree days are already over, you have kinda stressful job, you don't feel like playing hard games, or games where you have to concentrate a lot. Sometimes, you just want to come over to your place. make yourself a cup of tea and just relax on comfortable chair and just enjoy some kinda easy game. Preferably, with a mouse only controls.

But to be honest, you need to be ready that games will be strange, or better call them weird or maybe even creepy in some kinda way, cause variety of the titles, that can be played with mouse only is pretty limited and you should expect only chinese visual novels, or some nonsense clickers, or easy tower defense games, or some puzzle logic games.

Or it can be a game like Simulacra. I am not even sure how to call this genre, but what I really do know for sure - this game is completely stupid :) But, in a good funny way. They call it a simulation game, which is kinda fair, but doesn't cover the whole idea of this game. 

So, you start the game playing as not a man, not a woman, just whoever the hell you are, sex is not specified in this game. You found a smartphone and this is where the whole stupid part is about to start. I mean like, imagine you are that person who found a phone, okay? What you gonna do? For me it's completely obvious and easy - if phone is unlockable, you simply need to find someone with a name Mom, Dad, Sister, Boyfriend, Dog in a contact list, call one of them and let them know that you found this device and return it as soon as possible. In case phone is locked, you just need to go to the police station and give it to them for the further actions. Easy as that, don't you think so? But not for our protagonist! Instead all of this, he/she decides to play around with this phone and read messages/mail, check web history, tinder-alike app - I mean like literally everything what you don't have to do, when you find someone's phone, cause this is simply embarassing. For the whole game I had that feeling that I was playing as a retard, who had no job, no personal life, no entertainment sources, literally nothing, so that phone was a greatest relief ever. 

But, on the other hand, if that person wouldn't be that miserable and pathetic and wouldn't check that messages and videos on the camera roll - he wouldn't realize that phones belonged to someone who was desperately crying for help, stucked in some kinda danger. The more you click on that stupid phone the more stranger and uglier everything becomes, and you have to solve some kinda puzzles. All these puzzle things are more like "choose the right answer" in dialogues with a random people, talking about phone's owner, which is also a random person for you lol, which you shouldn't care about at all and all these combinations of answers lead you to different endings. Plus you have to recreate some corrupted messages, by putting words in the right order and renew corrupted photos by clicking on image pieces at the right order. Time to time, you will see ugly screamers on the phone, whose aim is to scarry you and like, to be honest, this one of the most ridiculous things in this game, cause I was laughing all the time when that was appearing on the screen, so I can't say that this game is a horror experience, it's more "wannabe horror game" , trying to be mysterious and creepy all the way ends up with a pretty shallow and a bit boring idea.

However, I can recommend this game. It brings you some fresh new experience and can be funny a little bit plus you can relax after a busy stressful day by just clicking on the dialogue options and solving pretty easy puzzles trying to figure out what the hell is going on there. 

So, to sum everything up!
You should grab this game if you: 

+ Feel like playing some easy game, where is no need for high concentration
+ Are a Black Mirror TV show fan and like all this paranoic idea about how it can be bad somewhere in the future for us with all these high-tech devices
+ Don't agree with me, that carrying a phone to the police station would be the best idea in this situation :)
+ Just looking for a new experience

Avoid this game if you:

- Don't like illogical games, with a stupid protagonist who has no idea what the hell is he doing 
- Have no desire to try something new and unusual

Enjoy!

I really don't like Steam's binary review system. I feel like "some" people would like this game... but to me it's suffering the following:

[list]
[*]Imbalance between (unintended?) camp and "horror" (mostly to do with a couple V/O performances)
[*]EXTREME over-reliance on jump-scares (which takes away from the investigation/mystery aspect)
[*]Some rough writing here and there
[*]Some "simulated choice" options (i.e. you HAVE to say things even if you wouldn't want to or it wouldn't make sense for your character to)
[*]Some REALLY obscure puzzles that have had to be answered by the developers themselves

All-in-all it's not a "bad" game... but it's a great "idea" with some execution misses.

That being said, if you love jump-scares and some weird screwed up imagery with "INTENSE" sound effects, etc. then you might dig this. If I were to arm-chair develop this, I would have held back on some of the jump scares to make them more effective than just annyoing, and leaned more into the "missing person investigation" aspect of things vs. bringing in the [spoiler]supernatural[/spoiler] elements so quickly. 

I think the overall presentation and mechanics are solid... none of my critiques of this game are "budget-related," but more about writing/pacing/etc. 

I'm gonna give this a "no" but with a big caveat, that I wouldn't recommend it to MOST people... I really think something special and unique is buried under the surface of this game, but I think maybe the development team just got a little to shy of the story itself and decided to overload it with trope-y jumpscare image-horror to cover it up a bit. 

I know these games are made by real people, and I empathize with the team behind this and hope they know that my "negative" review comes with a healthy does of optimisim that they have something great in them and look forward to their next go of it!

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is a found phone horror game. The premise of the game is that you (the unknown, nameless protagonist – but presumably *you*, the actual player) found a phone out on your front porch that belongs to a woman named Anna. There’s something off about the phone, though; it keeps glitching out, a number of the files on it are messed up, there’s some creepypasta-esque flashes of the screen changing to horrifying images – and of course it quickly becomes evident from the frantic messages you get from her boyfriend that Anna has gone missing.

The game’s basic premise is exploring Anna’s phone. You decrypt some images and text messages via very simple minigames, but most of it is a choices-matter narrative, as you interact with not only Anna’s boyfriend, but a funny guy named Taylor on Spark (a dating/hookup app that *totally* isn’t Tinder) who had been flirting with Anna, as well as messages from Ashley, Anna’s best friend. You browse a few in-game websites, make a few phone calls from phone numbers you find on them and hidden in various images, and gradually unravel the mystery of what happened to Anna over the course of the game.

This is something of a hybrid of a simple puzzle game and Telltale’s sort of narrative storytelling, where you have a list of dialogue choices and they influence how other characters react to you. There is actually a branching narrative – the choices you make actually influence which endings you can access as you try to save Anna, only to discover that things aren’t so easy, and how you treat the characters affects how they interact with you. If you’re a jerk to someone, they won’t trust you and will be a jerk back; if you’re nice to them, they’ll be more trusting. But at the same time, you can lie about who you are to various people in the game, and while sometimes they’ll figure it out, other times you’ll slot right in as a trusted person and be able to get what you need out of them.

Indeed, pretense is a major theme of the game – people aren’t quite who they present themselves to be online, and the fronts they put up often don’t match who they are (or, indeed, who they perceive themselves to be). Is Anna’s boyfriend really still together with her, or did they break up, and is he stalking her? There’s a bunch of sexual predators on Spark – is Taylor one of them? Does Ashley have ulterior motives in her friendship with Anna?

I’d like to say that the biggest flaw with this game is that the resolution is, perhaps, a bit on the nose. While I approve of this new age of horror, and coming up with a new spooky villain, I also didn’t feel like it did a good enough job of reinforcing the manipulation angle of social media, instead simply resorting to outright mind control, which was a lost opportunity.

However, I think the actual largest flaw with this game is that it is just okay. It is a clever idea, and there are some fun conceits in there, but I have to say at the end I was left feeling just lukewarm about it. When I play a game, or finish a game, I want a sense of satisfaction. But this was just sort of an experience I had. It wasn’t bad, but it wasn’t particularly excellent, either.

If you’ve never played a game like this before, and somehow got this for free or as part of a bundle, it’d be worth a spin to just try out something new. But at the same time, I’m left feeling like it’s hard to recommend that someone go out of their way to experience it, and when I recommend something, I want to actually be able to say to someone “Yes, you should go play this game.”

I wasn’t left with that feeling here, as while it is overall decent, it is all just a little bit flat, and the jump scares don’t manage to really carry the horror of the game very well.

[h1]A First Impression Review[/h1]

I shouldn't have liked this, but I did. I'm not a horror fan, but the concept was interesting enough to keep me hooked. It reminds me of the movie [i]Smile[/i]. It’s creepy and has some jumpscares that make you feel uncomfortable, but the intrigue of the puzzles actually sold me, despite not being a puzzle guy.

[h1]The Good[/h1]
- [b]Realistic Interface:[/b] Feels exactly like operating a normal Android phone. It's natural and easy to navigate.
- [b]Clever Puzzles:[/b] The difficulty is just right. You have to really think, like hunting through emails to find a mother’s maiden name for a password reset. 
- [b]The Drama:[/b] There is a good chunk of backstory in the messages. Reading through the texts, like the drama with the mom, felt realistic and wild. It adds weight to the mystery. It actually made me care about the missing women. 
- [b]Great Price:[/b] This game is cheap. It's under $10 at full price, and catching it on sale for under $2 is a big W.
- [b]Good Pacing:[/b] The game pushes you in the right direction. If you finish a task, you’ll get an alert letting you know exactly which app or person to investigate next.

[h1]The Not-So-Good[/h1]
- [b]Awkward Acting:[/b] The acting is a little awkward at times. I definitely laughed at a few moments, but it gets the job done and sells the story.

[b]TLDR:[/b] A neat mystery that makes you want to keep playing to see what happens next. If you like unique puzzles and can handle a bit of a creep factor, it’s worth it.

[b]Verdict:[/b]
☐ Skip It
☐ Buy it on Sale
☑️ Worth it at Full Price

After playing Sara is Missing and hearing about Simulacra through that purveyor of all things horror-related, Night Mind, I decided to check it out.  I was pleasantly surprised.  The story is much more developed compared to SiM, and I enjoyed exploring Anna's phone.  The concept of the game was much more interesting than SiM, though I feel like it could still be better developed and hope the devs continue with this idea.  While the text speak used by the main "players" of the game was perfectly realistic, I felt that the primary antagonist of the game [spoiler]Simulacra[/spoiler] would not have the spelling errors I encountered in that character's texting.  For instance, the character used "lead" instead of "led" and "it's" when "its" was intended.  I know, I know, others might not have noticed or been affected by this, but I felt that the character would not have made those errors.

Overall, the characters were better developed than SiM, definitely.  Anna was three-dimensional, and so were the characters we encountered.  Omitting Iris [spoiler]though of course allusions can be found in the website, thanks to the phone number and Morse Code[/spoiler], was a good decision.  I don't know if the plan is for DLC or sequels, but I look forward to a continuation of the Simulacra and/or Iris story-line, in this world where technology has a mind of its own.

For the devs:
[list]
[*]The ambiance is brilliant.  I love the room behind the phone, the lights flickering and the sounds around me.  It definitely creates an aura of suspense.
[*]As far as jump scares, I agree with Night Mind, unnecessary, kind of lame, and ineffective.
[*]What did solving the puzzles accomplish?  I mean, I don't know if I had to unscramble the photos and texts to progress, I just always do it to get it out of the way, but they don't, in the story, progress anything, really, [spoiler]until the Spark conversation with James[/spoiler].  Also they were really easy.  When you present me with a four-word scramble...come on.
[*]Where is this supposed to take place?  The accents were peculiar.  It seemed like you were aiming for American, but you were using British spellings, i.e. favourite.  Is it meant to take place in Canada?
[*]I did love the multiple endings, and felt much more invested in them than I did in SiM.  In particular, [spoiler]I just achieved the happy ending, and afterward, stared at the screen and said, "Did I just get possessed?  I think I just got possessed."[/spoiler]
[*][spoiler]Even if you're interviewing through text (for reasons?), why would you consider hiring a person to be a copywriter who makes that many spelling and grammatical errors?  I kept looking at my response options, and they were painful.  Yes, I understand you're not really applying and just trying to get information about James, but still.[/spoiler]
[/list]
All that being said, I do hope you continue and would love to play any other games set in this world.  If you appreciate nothing else from my review, let it be: less is more.  Subtle horror is better than overt horror.  The idea that somebody might be in the room with you, where you're holding that phone, or the idea that you might lower the phone and see, I don't know, a floating disembodied head, was so much more effective than momentary flashes of the screen turning into something scary.  And if [spoiler]the final image had been the player lowering the screen and something vague and shadowy, or even a representation of the Simulacra, being there, and then moving toward the screen if you simply must jump scare, it would have been better than the shift in Anna's picture.[/spoiler]  It's the suspense that gets you, not the actual scare.  You don't have the suspense before the jump scares on the phone, just an image shift.

Nevertheless, public who have reached this far (or TLDR), I do recommend this game.  It isn't a long game, but I've spent...7 hours in it so far?  And intend to spend more unlocking achievements.

SIMULACRA is a horror video game that has been highly anticipated by fans of the genre. However, after spending 1 hour playing the game, it has become clear to me that it falls far short of expectations.

One of the most disappointing aspects of SIMULACRA is the lack of polish in the graphics and sound design. The game is supposed to take place in the world of a smartphone, but the graphics are clunky and not at all realistic. The sound design is equally disappointing, with poorly implemented jump scares and music that doesn't fit the tone of the game.

The gameplay itself is also frustrating, with slow load times and confusing puzzles that are more frustrating than enjoyable. The story, which revolves around a missing person and the player's attempt to uncover the truth, is poorly executed and lacks the tension and scares that make a horror game truly effective.

In comparison to other horror games, SIMULACRA falls short in every aspect. The characters are one-dimensional and uninteresting, and the player's options for weapons and actions are limited. Even the in-game purchases feel like a desperate attempt to make up for the overall lack of quality in the game.

In my personal opinion, SIMULACRA is a major disappointment. It fails to deliver on the promise of an immersive horror experience and falls far short of the standard set by other games in the genre. I would not recommend this game to anyone and would give it a rating of 2/10.

tl;dr if you want a phone snooping game that is better than this (harder puzzles, better writing) + touches on some of the same themes, and don't mind it being non-horror, try out [b]Another Lost Phone: Laura's Story[/b].

I really like the conceit of a fake computer or phone as the setting for a mystery game, which is why a friend recommended I play this. However, I can't say that I would do the same.

The writing is riddled with typos and unnatural grammatical errors. Like, a lot of these characters aren't even convincingly fluent English speakers. (Also the way their only Black character is written is. reductive.) But it does have its moments that feel natural and compelling.

The acting is... bad. They sound like they're reading off a teleprompter one word at a time, rather than speaking a sentence, and the emotional reactions are not convincing. Worst of the bunch is, unfortunately, one of the two guys whose voice you hear the most. [spoiler](By which I mean Greg.)[/spoiler]

The characterization is weird? IDK, you spend most of your time talking to various brands of Men Who Are Creepy To Women, and it keeps asking you to side with at least one of them. [spoiler]By the way, one of them is a registered sex offender. And somehow, that's not even the reason he's creepy![/spoiler] Even your interactions with the women in the cast are usually about various aforementioned creepy men. [spoiler]The closeted lesbian coming out to (she believes) the woman she has a crush on? That conversation fails the Bechdel test, even if you consider the player impersonating Anna to be a "named woman."[/spoiler] So even though it's supposed to be about Anna, it's more accurately about men fighting over a woman-shaped trophy called Anna.
It may seem like I'm kind of harping on this but that's only because so MUCH of their characterization is either behaving inappropriately towards women or being belligerent to people in general. There's not much to go on without that.

As for the narrative, it was... railroady. I didn't feel like I was finding secrets because even if I found out something a little early, one of the guys would just tell me to do it later. The highly telegraphed railroading in the intro was actually my favorite UI moment in the game, but that was a lot more artful than the clumsy dialogue trees that all lead to a single point.
I did think the big bad was interesting, especially the part about [spoiler]how "a strong individual would simulate a better [life]" rather than live fully in a suboptimal one[/spoiler]. Though I felt like that theme of [spoiler]the appearance being more meaningful than the substance[/spoiler], while present in some parts of the game, such as [spoiler]reporting a colleague for harassment being an issue because it could reflect poorly on the company, or the folder of pictures of random women that Taylor just Has, Apparently[/spoiler], was underutilized. Which is odd, because... that's from your villain monologue—you HAVE to establish those themes in the story up to that point.

There's just a lot that could have been considerably better than it was.

[b]Playing status:[/b] 100% achievement, 4x + playthroughs
[b]Grindy Achievement(s):[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement(s):[/b] Yes (16 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement(s):[/b] No.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
You found a lost phone. Inside, you find someone asking for help. [b]SIMULACRA[/b] puts you in the shoe of a stranger who is trying to find the owner of a lost phone. Will you succeed or will you fail?

[b]Pros:[/b]
- 4 endings with slight story branches
- New game plus let you play the game with faster chat speed

[b]Cons:[/b]
- No manual save and extra save slot to make it easier to unlock all endings
- Not suitable for people who have issues with flashing lights

[b]Specs[/b]
Intel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to read a visual novel that was told through phone and chats, feel free to buy this game at a sale.[/i]

[hr][/hr]
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h3]Visuals[/h3]
As a game that is played out on a smartphone, the game does well to simulate the phone-like interface. It has a photo app, a contact book, a chat app - anything that you'll expect from a smartphone. Its functionality is limited tough. There is no option to switch between tabs nor a scroll bar on the right side of the screen to scroll the page faster.

[h3]Story[/h3]
The story is played out from series of chats. Expect a lot of typos and shortened words due to the informal context. This brings forth the characters' personality though, especially since everyone has a unique texting style from each other. Some information can also be retrieved by watching videos and receiving phone calls, although their voice is not expressive enough - it feels dragged out on purpose to make it easier for non-native English speakers to listen to. It does make them easier to hear, but it also kills their expression in the process.

Interface aside, the presentation helps with the storytelling. The glitchy screen and a few jumpscares help to set the mysterious vibe, while the surprising phone calls freak me out sometimes. It got toned down as you play the game, focusing more on the mysterious element. The writing was done well in regards to what's happening and sometimes, you will have several options to choose from. Despite giving the same outcome, the conversation will play out differently based on which option that you choose. However, some sentences are not flowing smoothly after choosing a certain option, giving you the impression that you chose the wrong one.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2466225479 

[h3]The Game[/h3]
[b]Gameplay[/b]
The gameplay is focused on chatting with people and exploring everything that is inside the phone that you used. As I said before, sometimes you will have to choose between several options to proceed. Some of them will affect the endings, some are not. Some old chat and photos will also be encrypted, allowing you to play a minigame to restore their state, which takes form in arranging photos or word. It's quite easy to finish although some words might be difficult to arrange sometimes.

Hints are usually provided whenever you are stuck. You can ask people to figure out what you are supposed to do and they will gladly help you out. However, I got stuck twice with no idea to proceed. Although one is expected since I never do well with puzzles that have vague rules, another feels like they don't give enough hints to solve.

[b]Length and Difficulty[/b]
I finished the game in ~4h, and proceed to replay the game several times to get all achievements. The new game+ helps a lot by providing a faster chat speed, allowing you to finish the game faster. However, you still need to wait for the voice-over near the ending to finish, and they talk very slowly. It was tiring to wait for them to finish talking and playing the game several times to unlock all four endings become not fun anymore. I wish there is an option to fast-forward the game at this point.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2466225684 

[b]Problems[/b]
Although the game has a phone-like interface, some quality of life features are missing, notably the option to switch tabs in the browser (or the option to keep existing tab), and the feature to start a video from a certain timestamp. There were also some occasions when I had to type some forms and I couldn't use the tab button in my keyboard to switch between text boxes. Lastly, there are some flashing lights near the ending - people who have issues with it might want to stay out of the game.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
For a visual novel game, it still can be enjoyed with people who don't like to read a wall of text. You might need to read a lot, but they are mostly in the form of short chats which shouldn't take long to finish. The story picks up an interesting topic that is enhanced with its mysterious vibe, and although the story feels weak at times, it still proves to be an enjoyable read.

A lost phone appears in your grasp out of nowhere. When you peaked inside, you discovered a creepy video of someone else either asking for assistance or not. In this game, you are abruptly connected to unusual occurrences that put the people nearby in possibly deadly situations.


[H1] Visual: [/H1]
The UX and UI of this game are quite straightforward but interesting in their aesthetic design. Every "app" in this game has been designed in such a way that it is simple to grasp what it is and what kind of hint it is intended to give the player. A genuine smartphone design is featured in the game, along with a number of in-game applications modeled after well-known mobile applications including social media, apps, emails and other type of apps.

[H1] Audio [/H1]
Simulacra's original soundtrack will play during the main menu; it isn't very remarkable, but it wonderfully complements the game. The audio in this game is quite loud and intentionally intended to jump scare the player during the game's horror scenes. The voice acting of the actors aren't really good either. There is nothing else really interesting other than that.


[H1] Gameplay: [/H1]

Simulacra provides a decent horror experience. In this game, the choices you made along the way are tightly linked to one another. This game includes a memo so that you won't get lost if you forgot about the tasks you "need" to do. However, aside from the primary objective—which is to find Anna—they are not really a must-do. It is sometimes necessary to stop doing what you "should" do (based on memo) in order to achieve a different result (that would suit the player better). These messages may appear insignificant, but they contain information that the player will need later on. The difference in outcome will not be visible right away because they are sometimes piling on top of one another before reaching the turning point. The player would also need to uncover puzzles and collectibles throughout the game. In this game, finding those kinds of items is necessary in order to progress the story, unlike other games where they are optional. The puzzles are straightforward to solve; they consist of jumbled words, and all you need to do is choose the appropriate text to complete it. 


[spoiler] If you want to complete the game to the fullest extent possible, you will need to play it more than once because various accomplishments can be unlocked separately and you can only choose one of them. As the game has a few but game-breaking bugs, it would be more practical and less risky to just concentrate on one path at a time rather than reloading a backup save just to get all the achievements in a single run. Although it is possible to do it with the game saves and try to squeeze everything up in one playthrough. I suggest making backup files after chatting with Ashley about "who's at fault."

[/spoiler]


[H1] Controls [/H1]

Keyboard and Mouse are the only way to play it.

[H1] Pricing [/H1]

Worth the price

TL;DR: Posting this review to help Steam out, since this game does NOT deserve such praise. Honestly, I would have been annoyed but said screw it if it was at "Very Positive"... but overwhelmingly positive? It literally does nothing new, innovative, or even good. In fact, I'd say the only thing it accomplished was copying things done many times before it in an absolutely terrible way. It was a slog to get through from beginning to end. I can honestly say it combined all the crappiest parts of horror movie trailers, the worst creepypastas and a s****y jigsaw puzzle together in a terrible phone-shaped package that lasted for WAY too long. It was 30 minutes of terrible content somehow stretched into 3 hours. In other words, if you get it in a bundle like me, go ahead and stop playing when you decide the moment is right. It's not going to get better.

Got this from the "Overwhelmingly Positive" Humble Bundle. How in the actual f*** is this game "Overwhelmingly Positive" ????? Kids review bomb awesome games on here all the time, and this managed to survive that for so long? I'm legitimately confused and concerned. Did this game get massive press in some media targeted specifically towards children, and somehow avoid literally everyone else? Did the people who hate it just not care enough to leave a review? Again, were on Steam, so how?????

On a particularly boring night, I played the entire damn thing. The first 5 minutes in I already knew it was going to be terrible, but stupidly I played on, hoping for something redeeming to happen to justify the positive reviews and my time wasted. That obviously didn't happen.

Bad writing, bad puzzles, atrocious "scares" (literally all jumps, flashing images and noises, and even then not a single f***ing one even managed a startled shutter from me, with volume annoyingly high), all set to an all-too-overplayed by now "hey, play this game on this device/OS/form of communication" gimmick that I'm frankly by now beyond tired of game developers using as a replacement for an interesting story/plot/writing (Stories Untold is the most recent game to do it RIGHT AFAIK). It was cool like the first 100 times maybe, but I'm over it.

I also want to point out, I don't think I have EVER seen good writing/plot in a game that has characters communicating through a messaging system, then has every character using terrible grammar, punctuation, etc. It bugs the hell out of me.
1.It's usually inconsistent. Some chatacters just spring in and out of it randomly.
2.We're not all 12. Some people actually care about that kind of stuff, so it doesn't make sense to have EVERYONE at some point talking like the slow, overly emotional kid in class.
3.It isn't 1995 anymore. It's one thing to have every character talk like that when they're using AOL Instant Messenger, but for chrissakes, you actually have to make an EFFORT to screw up grammar the way these characters do on a modern cellphone with autocorrect. Ugh.

Summary: For a horror/mystery/puzzle game, it is quite weak on each of the three elements. The least surprising mystery game I've played. Perhaps mainly because it blows its load from the start and spends the rest of the play time catching up with itself. Probably works better on mobile, as it seems made for a short attention span.

Pros:
- Basic concept is a cool commentary on social media and online dating
- A couple of surprising moments
- Some easter eggs and alternative paths give a bit of replay value

Cons:
- Storytelling is overstated and predictable
- Dialog is unconvincing, and I often didn't like my choices
- Game is linear and holds your hand almost the entire way. Some light puzzles, but otherwise no challenge, except unlocking a certain ending
- Acting is meh, supporting voice acting is mostly plain bad
- Annoying spelling errors are not always intentional

For examples of similar storytelling that really works: see Oxenfree and Doki Doki Literature Club.

!!!!! THIS REVIEW WILL *NOT* CONTAIN ANY STORY SPOILERS !!!!!

Simulacra is a short single-player experience that takes notes heavily from games such as "Her Story", "Emily is Away", and is eerily similar to "Sara is Missing". Having only played Simulacra, and not having played the others, I wouldn't feel right calling it merely a clone, and so I'll let it stand on its own.

Stemming originally from the point-and-click Adventure Game genres, these new detective-style games seem to be a welcome twist on an old idea. In Simulacra, you play, essentially, yourself. A strange phone has been left on your doorstep, and with seemingly nothing else to do for the day, you find yourself drawn into a mystery that only get stranger as more clues are discovered. 

The masterful design places you in control of the aforementioned phone, and in turn, of eight different phone apps, each more revealing than the last. The apps, meant to mimic modern day social media apps, are your wealth of information, and it shows (as I'm sure the creator intended) exactly how easy it can be to find someone using only a handful of these apps. As the story unravels, it becomes clear that something isn't quite right, and not everyone may be telling the truth. This game was packaged in with a Humble Bundle I purchased, and I was delighted with the experience, which I will outline below.

For a story told through different apps, I found that it (the story) never lost its pacing. As you hope with all good mysteries, I was completely enthralled, and intent on finding out exactly what happened. The lack of soundtrack is made up for with the addition of a host of spooky and scary sounds, ranging from low knocks on a nearby door, to terrifying schreeches from unlocked videos and glitches. This brings me to one of my gripes with the game: the minigame puzzles. 

While the minigames are a welcome break from the plethora of text in the game, I found their solutions to often be sort of convoluted. In fact, the only times that I felt unimmersed were the times I sat, hands on my head, attempting to solve a glorified word jumble, only to find that the answer was often unclear. Similarly, I had a difficult time figuring out the photograph puzzles, in which you stack and unstack layers of corrupted files until you find the ideal stacking formation that removes all corruption. Thankfully, these minigames were few and far in between, and most of my time was spent enjoying the different situations and obstacles in the way of my investigation. Hopping between apps in the game is as effortless as it is in real life, and made for very smooth transitions, and very little downtime as I progressed. 

The characters are pretty solid. It's a rich cast, and I was thankful to hear a notable quality in the performance of the actors. While there were one or two lines which made me cringe, the overall performances were fantastic, which bodes well for any completionists who plan to play multiple runs of this game, in order to live all the different outcomes. The voice acting was mostly really solid, and the video performances followed suit. I honestly could have done without all the spooky whispers and door knocks that were staggered throughout the playthrough. I understand their intention was to heighten the atmosphere of fear, but with the quality of the storytelling, I'm not sure that any additional atmosphere was really needed. Instead of shocking me, the rare jump scare attempts and 'spooky imagery' instead removed me from the story, and reminded me that I was, in fact, completely safe in my computer chair, instead of inside a strange house looming over a stranger's phone. Like the minigames, though, the attempted jump scares are sparsely placed within the game, and didn't detract from my overall enjoyment.

The total of my playtime consists of a single playthrough of the game, so use that as a measuring stick for how long a standard run will last. Despite enjoying the game very much, I do not think I'll replay it, mostly because I don't have a completionist mentality, and I was very satisfied from a single playthrough, but I definitely intend to do some research on what my decisions could have changed. If you're in the mood for a quick, but good story with compelling characters and a great design, than I'd highly recommend Simulacra. 

Thanks to the development team! You can tell a lot of love went into this game, and it was so much fun to play!

[h2] Simulacra Review: A Promising Start That Loses Its Way [/h2]

Simulacra is an intriguing, story-driven game that draws players in with its early mystery and atmosphere. However, as the game progresses, it begins to lose momentum, culminating in an abrupt and unsatisfying ending. Despite this, the game is still worth experiencing for those who enjoy narrative-focused titles, though it has a few notable shortcomings.

[h3] The Good: [/h3]

1) Compelling Start: From the beginning, Simulacra presents an engaging and mysterious premise that immediately captures the player's attention. The game’s atmosphere and pacing set the stage for an intriguing narrative.

2) Satisfying Puzzle Solving: For those with a keen eye for detail, solving the puzzles is rewarding. The game often challenges players to analyze small clues, and the sense of satisfaction upon uncovering key pieces of the story is one of its standout features.

3) Impactful Choices: The game does well in giving players the feeling that their choices matter. How you respond to certain characters affects their relationships with you, adding a layer of depth and emotional investment to the experience.

[h3] The Bad: [/h3]

1) Repetitive Gameplay: Unfortunately, the gameplay starts to feel repetitive as the game progresses. The entire experience is confined to a phone screen, and while this fits the premise, it can become tiresome over time, as the game rarely deviates from this formula.

2) Lack of Explanation for the Antagonist: The game’s main antagonist remains cryptic, with little explanation given for their motivations or origins. This leaves players with more questions than answers, which can feel frustrating for those who prefer a clear narrative.

3) Abrupt Ending: One of the biggest letdowns is the ending. For a story-based game, the conclusion should feel like a natural payoff, but instead, it feels rushed and unfinished, leaving many of the game’s intriguing threads unresolved. The game’s narrative feels carried more by its strong start than by its finale.

[h3] The Ugly: [/h3]

1) Repetitive Playthroughs: Replaying the game is a tedious process as players must start from scratch. There is no checkpoint system to revisit critical moments or alter the story’s outcome without going through the entire experience again. This makes multiple playthroughs feel like a chore.

2) Frustrating Achievements: Some of the achievements are either too obscure or require an unreasonable amount of time and patience to unlock. This might be off-putting for those who are not inclined to consult a guide or spend excessive hours grinding.

3) Annoying Sound Effects: While the sound design in Simulacra is generally effective, the game occasionally relies on loud, jarring noises in an attempt to startle the player. These moments feel cheap and detract from the otherwise immersive experience, disrupting the atmosphere rather than enhancing it.

[h3] Conclusion: 6/10 [/h3]

Simulacra has a lot to offer in terms of its mystery and narrative, especially for those who enjoy story-driven experiences. However, the lack of a satisfying ending, repetitive gameplay, and the absence of convenience features like a checkpoint system hold it back from being a truly great game. It’s definitely worth checking out if you’re a fan of mystery and story-focused titles, but if you’re sensitive to flashing lights or sudden loud noises, it might be best to approach with caution.

[b]SIMULACRA[/b] is detective visual novel with a hint of horror and a unique presentation and a couple of simple puzzles. The whole story unfolds on the screen of a phone lost by a missing girl. You start by looking through her videos, photos and chat history. There are even some interesting puzzles where you have to answer personal questions to restore password. But then the game shifts to the classic visual novel style, which uses chat windows instead of dialogue boxes. It becomes boring and the dialogue writing is kind of bad, expect stupid jokes and useless sentences. Another thing that made my walkthrough impossible are jumpscares, why put them in a game where you have to focus to read text? Somebody's gonna have a heart attack from this.

[b]Pros:[/b]
+ Unique presentation
+ Interesting 30-60 minutes of gameplay in the beginning

[b]Cons:[/b]
- Jumpscares
- Boring dialogue that tries too much to be funny
- Not much in terms of gameplay

The game has a great concept, looking through personal stuff to figure out what happened is interesting, but the game ditches it in less than an hour. If you were interested in the game because of it, you should try [b]Telling Lies[/b], which explores this same idea, but sticks to it for the whole game.

review_text_raw:
Great idea, but bad execution. A for effort but C on the result.

PROS:
- Technical polish. The UI looks good and the videos, picture and audio are of good quality.
- The developers did seem to put their heart into this. It is not easy to make games involving so much detail, actors and voice work
- Interesting concept. While not original, piercing the story together through different apps on the phone was neat
- Some puzzles were neat like finding a phone number hidden in Twitter posts or creating a specific Tinder profile, because they fit the concept of the game really well

CONS:
- All the characters are downright unlikable.. I didn't care for Anna one bit and if there was an ending to kill them all off I would have took it. And when I mean all, I really mean all. Every single one, including her mother and the HR lady. I guess only the cat gets a pass and even then I'm not sure
- Unrealistic voice work. Most characters speak very unnaturally. The biggest offender being Greg who talks like he is in a kid's anime
- You can only speak to people when they are online, but they always pop up immediately when you need them to make progress, making it very obvious you are playing a videogame. A few seconds delay would have done wonders for the immersion
- Repetitive gameplay. Most of the time you will be doing the same "construct a phrase" or "remake a picture" puzzle and the whole cycle of restoring the phone data should have only happened once.
- Cheap cheap "horror" with zero atmosphere but instead lots of dumb jump-scares (really really a lot) and in-your-face weirdness. No subtlety whatsoever, making the "horror" cheap, pointless and braindead
- The ending. I felt dumber after the villain reveal and finished the game. Not sure I can put up with another run to see the other endings. I was expecting something stupid, but this worse than I expected

They really should have either cut the "horror" and gone full psychological crime thriller (which would have worked really well with the gameplay) or just go full ham and make the weirdness go on through the whole experience escalating more and more.
Instead you get a detective story ruined by awful jump scares or a horror story bogged down by boring detectice work. I would prefer the former as the later was really really bad, inspired by the worst horror movies the '10s had to offer.

I can forgive the bad dialogues and bad acting due to being an indie game, but I would suggest the developers to at least not use outdated memes in people's speech.

Only buy it on sale and expect a mediocre experience that pisses you off because it had the potential to be much better.

In the Simulacra games, you’re put into the role of a person who gets in possession of a mobile phone, and you have to solve puzzles in order to figure out what happened to its original owner. I’m lumping these two games together because even though their narratives aren’t connected to any great degree, the overall concept and gameplay is identical for both games.

In general, the Simulacra games remind me a lot of how the Orwell games work, in the sense that much of what you do is rifle through personal data. What’s different is that in these games you’re an active participant and not just an observer, so you get to talk to various characters directly, instead of just listening into their conversations.

Now just finding a phone and looking through its contents isn’t that interesting, most people in general aren’t interesting. But both games start with video messages from the original owners that indicate that something sinister is going on, and that’s where the FMV sequences come into play. 

For what it’s worth, these sequences aren’t played out of some misguided, ironic attempt at nostalgia like many other FMV games. It’s more just a representation of how we use our phones in real life. Video isn’t just a gimmick here, it’s part of what the games need to have in order to tell their stories.

Unfortunately, the acting during these FMV sequences isn’t that great. The first game does come off a bit better because it’s mostly centered around online dating, so there are only a few videos or instances of video calls that happen, but the second game targets influencer culture, where video plays a much bigger role. And there are also video sequences that happen outside of the context of the phone, because this is a sequel and I guess that’s a way of telling your customers that it’s worth buying another one because it has more stuff than the previous one. As a result, the unconvincing acting takes up much more runtime.

And I do have to say that the second game really hams it up a notch. It’s difficult to tell if the acting quality is intentional, since the second game is a rather scathing takedown of influencer culture, it could also be a jab at the terrible acting influencers employ during their fake drama.

The writing is pretty decent for the most part. I mean, these are cheesy horror games mostly about millennials, so you’re not really expecting F. Scott Fitzgerald quality stuff here, but it still manages to convey a sense of personality, even to some of the characters whose voices you never get to hear. Though I have to say that the second game has this weird idea of making every single character you have to investigate a complete as[i][/i]shole. I guess this comes with the territory for professional influencers. But if you, like me, watch cheesy 80’s slasher movies in order to see smug teenagers die in creative ways without having to empathize with them, it’s weird for the game to then turn around and give you a bad ending for wanting to punish these self-centered jerks. To get the good ending and also not miss out on a bunch of actual puzzles and therefore content, you have to stroke their egos quite a bit and metaphorically appeal to the power of friendship to solve the mystery.

review_text_raw:
[b]Simulacra[/b] is a "found phone" game—a genre where players uncover clues after discovering a stranger's lost smartphone. While the concept has gained popularity in the last decade, games have experimented with faux interfaces mimicking imagined technology for years. I remember playing Mean Streets and the officially licensed X-Files game, both of which attempted something similar.

In Simulacra, you navigate the protagonist's phone within the game's tightly controlled framework, piecing together what happened to its owner. I was initially drawn to the game due to the resurgence of modern full-motion video (FMV) storytelling. Having enjoyed 2015's Her Story, I expected a similar experience. While Simulacra integrates FMV clips effectively, its "found phone" premise was far less compelling to me. I think I hit an audience mismatch—I’m simply not a fan of smartphones. Since I don't particularly enjoy using my own phone, the idea of rifling through someone else’s was unappealing. I played on my laptop and embarrassingly took about a third of the game to realize that it was undoubtedly designed to be played on a smartphone—duh.

The protagonist, Anna, feels like a generic twenty-something woman struggling with rocky relationships, an unfulfilling job, and repeated rejections in her academic and professional pursuits. [spoiler]She has a non-binary best friend, which the game seemingly frames as a revelation, but it’s so heavily telegraphed that it falls into cliché territory.[/spoiler] In fact, Anna herself is a walking cliché, as is the familiar "technology is evil" theme—an overused trope in uninspired sci-fi narratives. After seeing it so often, it no longer has much impact for me.

The game’s title did surprise me. Before playing, I had never encountered the terms "Simulacra" or "Simulacrum," which piqued my curiosity. Midway through, I looked up the meaning, wondering why a game about a woman's lost phone would have such a name. Ah, crap—spoilers.

As for gameplay, Simulacra offers little freedom. Players must follow rigidly scripted conversations in a precise order to unlock new options and clues. While there are minor choices in how you interact with Anna’s close friends, they ultimately boil down to a few dialogue changes that determine which of the five endings you get—most of which depend on choices made in the last 10% of the game. That said, I appreciated that I could make all the necessary connections without resorting to a guide or hints. That sense of progress and accomplishment is something lacking in other puzzle or adventure games.

Overall, Simulacra is predictable but not necessarily bad. The FMV clips are well-integrated, Wendy Van Horen Carneiro delivers a solid performance as the wronged damsel in distress, and the faux-phone interface is thoughtfully designed. I give it a [b]3 out of 5[/b]—though the game is clearly aimed at a different audience than me, so others may find it more engaging.

review_text_raw:
If you're only just now hearing about Simulacra because it got a sequel, don't feel bad... you're not alone. Somehow this sci-fi horror simulation game ended up flying under the radar of a lot of people until recently. It comes from Kaigan Games, the creators of Sarah Is Missing; a title unavailable on Steam, but is playable for free over on Itch.io. It's a very similar predecessor to Simulacra, and perhaps it helped to serve as an unrefined beta for this more solid-feeling experience.

To say much about the story is to give away the entire game, so to give a very brief synopsis... you found a phone on your doorstep. Opening and accessing its apps leads you to discover that it was previously owned by a girl named Anna. After some digging around in the contents of the device and chatting with her boyfriend and best friend, you realize that Anna has gone missing, and she has been missing for some time. You'll have to recover data, browse photos and videos, and consult with others who were in touch with Anna before her disappearance in order to try and figure out what happened to her, and if you're capable of finding her and saving her life.

The entire game centers around Anna's phone; there's never a time where you will not be using it. The developers have done an outstanding job with creating an entire, believable world within the device; it's fabulously easy to slip into the realm of Simulacra and lose hours of time just checking out all of the dating profiles, work e-mails, and off-beat articles that were added to make the game just that much more realistic. There are several of these websites and news articles to read through, handfuls of in-depth e-mails, tons of selfies of Anna that show off her life and interests, and apps that simulate ones that most of us have installed on our own phones. Of course, a lot of these things are essential components to solving little detective-style puzzles, but there's also a good portion that is just there for entertainment. The game feels like an expansive ARG (alternate reality game), and if one were to play this title on an actual mobile device then the immersion would be surreal.

There are very few areas here that need any work, but the voice acting is one of them. A lot of the voice-overs, especially for Anna's boyfriend, are just embarrassingly cringe-worthy. The acting seen in many of the videos is also pretty bad, but not as bad as the voice work. Those are the only real complaints here, and they're honestly just nitpicky as they can be overlooked with ease. The game's interface is user-friendly, there's a great speed up option unlocked after beating the story once so that players can quickly get to the other four endings (as there are five) and explore different dialogue options, and there's enough small little horror elements to keep the gameplay tense throughout the first playthrough. Overall, it's one of the best casual, story-based sci-fi horror experiences out there right now.

Simulacra is one of those rare gems that manages to slip under the radar of most people; despite being out for almost three years and having over 1,000 reviews on Steam. It's the perfect blend of technology-based sci-fi and subtle horror, in the same vein of TV shows like Black Mirror and Dark Net. While its premise might sound cheesy, this title has some of the most immersive content that I've ever personally witnessed in the thousands of games that I've played. It borders on being an ARG, as there is an incredible level of attention to detail within every app, website, and chat that you'll delve into. Though an initial playthrough only takes about four hours, that time will be sucked away and you'll be left wondering how the hell it got so late, so fast. You'll also be left craving more, so definitely check out Sarah Is Missing and Simulacra 2 afterwards.

Simulacra is a game about something. I'm not really sure what, since the game is practically foreshadowing its own inability to deliver on its buildup in many places, and the solution to the mystery had me wondering why there even was a mystery to solve, being that it was something which had little to do with anything that exists in the real world (though there is doubtless some deep philosophical meaning behind the Ghost of Facebook Profiles Past throwing someone off a building for not having enough followers on MySpace).
The story is told through a cast of characters, inlcuding, but not limited to: A man who you can convince to commit corporate espionage and B&E in one sentence each, a sex offender who couldn't shut up to save his life, and the girl who went missing, has her entire character arc revealed in chapter one and never gets any more developement aside from us finding out that everything she did was, in fact, understandable, if rude. All of these reserved seats on the short bus are caught up in a missing person case, but have to do it through the player character, who has his own character, and who can't count to his own IQ. The story is told through tweedle dee and tweedle dum figuring out ways to get more evidence, and the protagonist actually doing it.
The dialogue system is both good and bad. It's bad because the dialogue was bootlegged from Fallout 4, and rarely had the thing I wanted to say, and good in that they actaully manage to do more with it than Bethesda ever did. As stated, the two stooges figure out new ways to attack the case and figure things out, and you actaully do it with puzzling that ranges from "good" to "really bad". There are puzzles where you put together images such that htere's no corruption, which I liked,  puzzles where you unscramble sentences, which were rarely necessary but also rarely obnoxious, and there were puzzles where you have an article to draw information from, but the information in the article is more wrong than the information Bill Cosby the 2nd pulls out of thin air.
Don't worry about the horror elements, it's just a few loud noises and distorted images. So we have a game where the horror is token, the story is confusing, and the characters are dumb and/or pricks. It's technically perfectly adequate, but so are virtually all visual novels, and what extra this does amounts to set decoration. 3/10, since someone who is willing to not think too hard might find it artistically brilliant.

[b]Last time I pick up a random phone.[/b]

One day, you find a phone just sitting on your doorstep. Like anybody else, you decide to snoop through the phone either to figure out who the owner is so you can return it or just because you can. However, this turns into a much more complicated situation. The first tip off is that while you are blocked by a lock screen, the phone glitches so you can get into it. I don’t know about anybody else, but I wouldn’t have looked through it after that. Anyway, you soon find out that the phone’s owner is Anna and she has recently gone missing. Thus, you decide to look through her phone activity and talk to her friends and acquaintances in an attempt to find her before it’s too late.

There are some puzzles here with the most frequent puzzle you’ll come across involves unscrambling text messages and photos. For texts, you’ll have to order the words in the right order. Photos are more complicated as you’re given several fragments to piece together, but you can’t have any part that is glitched. So you’ll have to figure out which order will allow all glitched out parts to be replaced with the picture. The other puzzle you’ll come across involve you gathering information through either the sites Anna frequented or through her friends. The only problem I had was that some messages had more than one way that it could make sense and that there is an instance where you’re expected to remember certain facts since you can’t go and look for the information.

The acting is average, with Anna’s actress being the stand out, with hilariously bad parts (aka all of Greg’s voice lines) sprinkled in. Voice acting mainly comes through Anna’s vlogs, audio text messages, and phone calls. What doesn’t exactly make sense are the phone calls. At certain points in the story, you’ll get a phone call from one of the characters and you’ll have to answer it (or they’ll keep calling/story won’t continue). Of course, you can’t answer back and when that character asks why you don’t talk back, the excuse is that you can’t make out what they’re saying (despite you being able to hear them fine). I’d rather have the excuse either be that you guess the mic got broken before you found it (which can also imply that whatever is making the phone glitch is causing the mic to stop working) or it auto sends them to voicemail. [spoiler]It doesn’t make sense even more when a police officer actually calls you but assume he’s leaving a voicemail despite not hearing “leave a message after the beep”.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]Also, I just couldn’t help but laugh at the look she gives Taylor in the ending where both of them live.[/spoiler]

Simulacra has four endings each with their own requirements. While you can’t jump to a specific section of the game, you’ll be able to speed things up on your next playthroughs through Begin+. It won’t take long to build up the requirements you need, but the last sequence plays at the same speed.

While Simulacra isn’t perfect, it’s still worth it to experience it yourself, whether it be on PC or on your phone to get the maximum immersion you can. I did find the phone aspect convincing for the most part, didn’t mind that glitches were used to freak you out (though others might not like it), and liked how they filled in the empty space with a room with ambient noises chiming in. There are even some subtle moments here, like the phone’s background changing. The only thing that really messes with immersion is some of the voice acting.
